title: Raga Gauri
hook: the largest section of the Granth (ang 151), earnest and deep

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Majh, and your line was letters of longing. Did you write your three lines? Today, the third raga, and a long one. Day one thousand seventy.

Last thing at night, in the Sohila, the first hymn carries a heading that's easy to pass right over: Raag Gauri Deepaki. So anyone who has read the bedtime prayer has already seen Gauri named. Its main home, though, is further on. On ang one hundred fifty-one the Gauri section begins, and then it keeps going, page after page after page. The book names a mood, and then it stays inside that mood for a long walk. Today: Raga Gauri.
screen: `THE SOHILA: RAAG GAURI DEEPAKI.` → `ANG 151: THE GAURI SECTION.` → `PAGE AFTER PAGE AFTER PAGE.`

segments.voice: Gauri is the raga of the serious conversation. Musical tradition hears it as earnest and deep, a mood for things that matter and won't be rushed: not grief, exactly, and not joy, but attention. Then look at the headings, because Gauri comes in shades. The section opens with Gauri Guarairi. Turn the pages and you'll find Gauri Purbi, Gauri Bairagan, Gauri Cheti, Gauri Majh, Gauri Deepaki, each name a different color of the same raga, written above the hymns it carries. It's as if one deep voice could speak in many tones. And it isn't one voice speaking. The Gurus' hymns fill the first long stretch. Then Kabir's hymns in Gauri fill a long stretch of pages of their own, with Namdev and Ravidas after. One taste of the earnestness: a hymn of Guru Tegh Bahadur in Gauri, on ang two hundred nineteen. O holy ones, it says in paraphrase, give up the pride of the mind. Run, day and night, from lust and anger and bad company. There's no ornament in it. Just a plain instruction, said with the weight of someone who means it. That's the Gauri sound: no hurry, no show, a voice leaning in close to say the true thing. Why so much of the Granth in this one raga? The text doesn't say, and it's fine to leave the question open. But it's easy to notice that so much of what the Gurus said about the mind, pride, the Name, death and peace found a home in a raga built for saying serious things. That's today's line: earnest and deep. Tomorrow, two great compositions that live here.
screen: `GAURI: THE SERIOUS CONVERSATION.` · `ONE RAGA, MANY SHADES.` · `GIVE UP THE PRIDE OF THE MIND.` · then, large: `EARNEST AND DEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Gauri. If you can find a shabad sung in Raag Gauri, play it now, and listen for the earnestness before the words: a melody that leans in rather than shows off. If there's no recording near you, make the sit itself earnest. Sit up a little straighter. Let one serious thing come to mind, a choice, a worry, a person, and don't argue with it or solve it. Just give it your full attention, the way Gauri gives its words full attention. When the mind wanders, come back without scolding. If you pray, you can set that one serious thing beside a quiet Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Raga Gauri. The third raga section of the Granth, beginning on ang one hundred fifty-one and running on for page after page, in many named shades, heard as earnest and deep. Today's word.
Your line: earnest and deep. Today, have one conversation at Gauri's pace: no phone, no hurry, and say the true thing plainly. Day one thousand seventy.

howItsDone: Gauri hymns are sung in kirtan in the raga named in their headings, and Sikhs who say the Kirtan Sohila at night meet Gauri in its first hymn, headed Raag Gauri Deepaki.

what a scholar hears: the Gauri section runs from Ang 151 to Ang 346, in sub-forms such as Gauri Guarairi, Purbi, Bairagan, Cheti, Majh and Deepaki, with the Gurus' hymns followed by those of Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas.
